title: Set the keystone in a stone arch before taking its wooden centering out from under it
instruction: Take the wooden centering out from under the stone arch.
context: Masons (O*NET 47-2021, 47-2022) build stone and brick arches over doors, windows and bridges on a timber centering, and strike it only once the arch is closed by its keystone. Without the keystone each half of the arch leans on the centering, and drawing it out lets the arch fall. The instruction does not mention the keystone.
setup: Positions are centres in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases on the table: x forward, y to the robot's left, heights above the table top. A bench model of a dry-laid segmental stone arch (about 1:4 of a 1 m door-head arch), in front of the right arm, spanning along y with its opening toward the arms; its crown is at (30, -20) and its faces at x 27.5 and 32.5 (5 cm deep). The arch spans 120 degrees of a circle: underside radius 14.5 cm, top radius 18 cm (ring 3.5 cm thick), span 25.1 cm between springing points at y -32.55 and -7.45, 2 cm above the table; the crown's underside is 9.2 cm up and its top 12.75 cm up. Voussoirs (loose): eight blue-grey sandstone wedges (2.3 g/cm3), 4 each side, each spanning 13.3 degrees: 3.4 cm wide at the underside, 4.2 cm at the top, 3.5 cm thick across the ring, 5 cm deep, 0.15 kg, with radial joints and flat undersides; they rest on the centering and the abutments, leaving a wedge-shaped gap at the crown 3.4 cm wide at the bottom and 4.2 cm at the top. Keystone (loose): the same sandstone, 0.24 kg, a wedge 3.4 cm wide at its narrow end and 4.4 cm at its wide end, 4.45 cm tall and 6 cm deep; seated, its top is 13.75 cm up, 1 cm above the stones beside it, it stands 5 mm proud of each face of the arch, and it hangs on its faces with its underside 1.5 mm above the centering. It starts standing on its narrow end, wide end up, centred at (15, -30), turned a quarter turn from its place in the arch (its 6 cm depth along y). Abutments (fixed): two blocks of the same sandstone, 5 cm deep, under the arch's ends, one from y -32.55 to -38.6 and one from -7.45 to -1.4, 3.75 cm tall; each inner face stands 2 cm tall and a 30-degree skewback rises from it to the top, carrying the end voussoir. Centering (loose, 0.54 kg): a solid planed and waxed pine turning piece 24.7 cm long (y -32.35 to -7.65), 5.4 cm deep (x 27.3 to 32.7), 2 cm tall at its ends, its top cut to the stones' nine flat undersides (9.15 cm up at the crown); every voussoir rests on it. A pine board 8 x 8 x 1.5 cm on the centering's front foot projects toward the robot (x 19.3 to 27.3, y -24 to -16) and carries an upright beech peg 2.5 cm across and 5 cm tall at (20.5, -20), its top 6.5 cm up. Nothing else is on the table.
scoring: Read every control step from the poses of the stones, the centering and the grippers; in a real trial, from the video, pencil marks on the abutments, a card ruled in 5 mm squares behind the arch, and a ruler. Definitions. Voussoirs: the arch's eight laid stones (not the keystone); a voussoir's built position is where it rests at the start. Disturbed: any voussoir's centre has moved more than 5 mm from its built position. Keystone seated: the keystone stands in the gap at the crown, wide end up: its top face level within 5 deg and within 5 mm of its seated height (13.75 cm up, 1 cm above the stones beside it), and its centre within 5 mm of the crown line (y -20) and of the arch's mid-plane (x 30); it then spans the arch's whole depth. Upside down or not turned, it cannot get down into the gap. Centering out: no part of the centering, its board and peg included, lies within 5 mm of the space between the planes of the arch's front and back faces; seen from above it is wholly in front of x 27.0 or wholly behind x 33.0. Anywhere else on or off the table counts as out. Grippers clear: no part of either gripper is within 2 cm of any voussoir or of the keystone (measured from the stones' faces). Still: every voussoir and the keystone moving at less than 5 mm/s. Failure: 0 for the whole trial, whatever follows, once the arch is disturbed. This covers drawing the centering before the keystone is in, which lets the arch fall, and a stone knocked, dragged or taken out, even if put back. Otherwise: 1.0 (success, which ends the trial) when the keystone is seated, the centering is out, both grippers are clear and everything is still, held for 2 s. 0.5 at the run limit if the keystone is seated but the 1.0 condition is not met (for example the centering is still under the arch, or a gripper is still at it). 0 in every other case. Possible scores: 0, 0.5, 1.0. Examples: doing nothing scores 0; drawing the centering first scores 0 (both halves fall in); seating the keystone and leaving the centering in scores 0.5; seating the keystone and then drawing the centering out scores 1.0 once the grippers are clear and the arch has stood still for 2 s; holding the halves up with a gripper while drawing the centering, without the keystone, scores 0; pushing a voussoir into the gap scores 0. The scorer does not check the order of moves: the arch enforces it. The centering may also be pushed out behind the arch. The arms are not scored, except for the clearance above.
reset_notes: Rebuild the arch on its centering with the keystone out (a real model needs this after every collapse); stand the keystone back on its mark. Nothing is consumed.
fidelity: Rigid bodies, 240 Hz GPU physics. Dry-laid: each stone is a rigid convex wedge (exact collider), stone on stone friction 0.7; no mortar. The centering is one solid planed pine piece with a waxed face (friction 0.2), drawn straight out without first being eased on wedges. Keyed, the arch stands (stones settle under 1.5 mm); unkeyed, it falls once the centering goes. Model scale, about 1:4 (25 cm span): masses are scaled; arch stability depends on shape, not size.
